title: Design a URL shortener
source: Original, inspired by the URL shortener chapter of donnemartin/system-design-primer (GitHub)
prompt: Design a service like bit.ly. Users submit a long URL and get a short one. Visiting the short URL redirects to the original.
functional: Create a short URL for a long URL
Redirect a short URL to the original long URL
Users can optionally pick a custom alias
non_functional: Redirects must be fast (under 100 ms at the server)
The service must stay available even if one server fails
Short links should not be easy to guess
scale: Read to write ratio about 100 to 1

components.name: Load balancer or API gateway
components.why: spreads traffic over many app servers and gives one entry point

components.name: Application servers
components.why: handle create and redirect requests

components.name: Database for URL mappings
components.why: stores short code to long URL mappings for 5 years

components.name: Cache for hot links
components.why: reads outnumber writes 100 to 1, so popular links should be served from memory

components.name: Short code generator
components.why: creates unique short codes without collisions

pitfalls: Hashing the long URL without handling collisions
Using a single database server with no replication for a service that must stay available
Ignoring the 100 to 1 read to write ratio, so no cache is drawn
Storage arithmetic that does not match the stated scale (100M per month for 5 years is about 6 billion records)
Redirects drawn to go through a slow path such as a full database scan for every request
Arrows drawn without a clear direction for who calls whom

title: Design a rate limiter
source: Original, inspired by the rate limiter discussions in ByteByteGo's system design videos (YouTube)
prompt: Design a rate limiter that protects a public API. It limits how many requests each user or API key can make in a time window, and rejects the extra requests.
functional: Limit requests per user or API key
Return HTTP 429 with a retry-after header when a limit is hit
Limits can be set per endpoint and changed without a deploy
non_functional: Adds under 5 ms to each request
Works the same across many app servers
If the limiter's store fails, legitimate traffic still gets through (fail open)
scale: 50,000 requests per second across the platform
Limit rules change a few times per day

components.name: Rate limiter component
components.why: the place where each request is counted and accepted or rejected

components.name: Shared counter store
components.why: counts must be shared across app servers, so they cannot live in each server's memory

components.name: Rules or config service
components.why: limits per endpoint change without a deploy

components.name: Load balancer or API gateway
components.why: the usual place to enforce limits before traffic reaches the servers

pitfalls: Keeping counters in each app server's memory, so limits are not shared
Counting every request in a relational database, which is too slow at 50,000 requests per second
Non-atomic read then write on the counter, which lets bursts slip past the limit
Fixed windows with no mention of the burst at the edge of each window
No behaviour when the counter store is down (fail open or closed is not stated)

title: Design a chat app like WhatsApp
source: Original, inspired by the chat system design walkthroughs in ByteByteGo (YouTube) and donnemartin/system-design-primer (GitHub)
prompt: Design a messaging app with one-to-one and group chats. Messages arrive in real time on every device, and a user can see their history on a new phone.
functional: One-to-one and group chats (up to 500 people)
Messages delivered in real time when the receiver is online
Messages reach offline users when they come back, with a push notification
Message history is available on a new device
non_functional: Delivery under 200 ms on a good network
No message is lost, even if a server fails
Messages stay in order within a chat
scale: About 40 messages per daily active user, so about 23,000 messages per second on average and three times that at peak
Group chats of up to 500 people

components.name: Real-time connection gateway
components.why: keeps a persistent connection open for live messages instead of polling

components.name: Message store
components.why: keeps every message so history can be loaded on a new device

components.name: Message queue or pub/sub
components.why: decouples sending from delivery and fans out to group members

components.name: Push notification service
components.why: reaches offline users

components.name: Presence or recent message cache
components.why: shows who is online and serves recent messages quickly

pitfalls: Polling the server for new messages instead of keeping a persistent connection
No acknowledgement or retry, so messages can be lost
Storing all messages in one database with no partitioning by chat
Group fan-out not considered: one message to a 500-person group is 500 deliveries
Offline users and push notifications not drawn at all
Ordering not addressed, so replies can appear before the message they answer

title: Design a company FAQ assistant (RAG)
source: Original, inspired by retrieval-augmented generation tutorials that are common on Reddit (r/MachineLearning, r/LocalLLaMA) and YouTube
prompt: Design an assistant that answers employee questions from the company's internal documents (HR policies, IT guides, product docs). Every answer must point to the document it came from.
functional: Answer questions in plain language from internal documents
Show the source document and section for each answer
Say clearly when the documents do not contain the answer
Only use documents the asking employee is allowed to see
non_functional: First words of the answer appear within 2 seconds
Answers stay grounded in the documents, not the model's memory
New or changed documents appear in answers within a day
scale: 500 employees, peak of 20 questions per minute
Documents updated about once a day

components.name: Document ingestion pipeline
components.why: turns documents into searchable chunks and keeps them up to date

components.name: Embedding model
components.why: turns chunks and questions into vectors so they can be matched by meaning

components.name: Vector database
components.why: finds the most relevant chunks for a question

components.name: LLM for answer generation
components.why: writes the answer from the retrieved chunks

components.name: Access control check
components.why: stops employees seeing documents they should not

pitfalls: Asking the LLM without retrieval, so answers come from its memory
No source citations shown with the answer
Access control applied after retrieval, or not at all, so restricted content leaks into answers
No re-indexing when documents change, so answers go stale
Changing the embedding model without re-embedding the whole corpus
No behaviour for questions the documents cannot answer

title: Design an AI code review bot for pull requests
source: Original, inspired by AI code review tools discussed on Reddit (r/programming, r/ExperiencedDevs) and in YouTube system design talks
prompt: Design a bot that reviews every new pull request on the company's Git host and posts inline comments on the changed lines with suggested fixes.
functional: Review each new pull request and each new push to it
Post inline comments on the changed lines only
Skip generated files and lockfiles
Let developers mark a comment as not useful
non_functional: Review posted within 5 minutes of the push
The same comment is never posted twice, even if a webhook is delivered twice
Code only goes to the company's approved model provider
scale: 2,000 developers, about 300 pull requests per day
Peak of 40 pull requests per hour

components.name: Webhook receiver
components.why: receives new pull request and push events from the Git host

components.name: Job queue and workers
components.why: keeps the webhook fast and lets slow model calls run in the background

components.name: Diff fetcher
components.why: gets only the changed lines and surrounding context to send to the model

components.name: LLM review service
components.why: produces the review comments

components.name: Comment poster and store
components.why: posts comments and records what was posted, so nothing is duplicated

pitfalls: Sending the whole repository to the model instead of the changed files and their context
Running the model inside the webhook handler, so requests time out
No idempotency, so a redelivered webhook posts duplicate comments
No rate limit on the Git host's API when posting many comments
Private code sent to an external model with no approval or data policy drawn
Ignoring the 300 pull requests per day scale when sizing workers

title: Design a multi-provider LLM gateway
source: Original, inspired by the LLM gateway and routing discussions in engineering blogs shared on Reddit and YouTube
prompt: Design an internal gateway that gives every product team one API to call many LLM providers. It handles routing, failover, caching, quotas by team, and usage reports.
functional: One API for many model providers
Automatic failover to another provider when one fails or is rate limited
Per-team quotas and monthly budgets
Streaming responses token by token
Usage reports per team and per model
non_functional: The gateway adds under 50 ms of overhead
One provider outage causes no user-visible errors
Prompts with personal data are never written to logs in plain text
scale: Average request has 1,500 input tokens and 500 output tokens

components.name: Routing and failover
components.why: chooses a provider and moves to another when one fails

components.name: Response cache
components.why: saves cost and latency for repeated requests

components.name: Quota and budget service
components.why: enforces per-team limits in tokens, not just request counts

components.name: Provider adapters
components.why: translate one request format to each provider's API

components.name: Usage metering and logs
components.why: records tokens and cost per team for reports and budgets

pitfalls: Failover drawn with no health check, so requests keep going to a dead provider
Cache key missing the model and parameters, so answers leak across models
Quotas counted in requests instead of tokens, so cost is not controlled
Streaming buffered in full before returning, which defeats streaming
Full prompts with personal data stored in logs
A single gateway instance with no horizontal scaling for 2,000 requests per second
